## cadmpeg

**cadmpeg** — the file: a SolidWorks, CATIA, Inventor, Creo, NX, Fusion, FreeCAD, Rhino or IGES document read into one format-neutral CAD document, and written back out.

### `cadmpeg_formats` — What this build reads and writes

The input formats compiled into this build, each with the file extensions it claims, and the output formats it can write. A format that is not listed cannot be read here, whatever the file is called.

It takes no arguments.

**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `cadmpeg_inspect` — What is in a CAD file, and how faithfully it was read

Opens a CAD file — native or STEP — and answers its decode report: the dialect it was read as, what was transferred, and every loss with its reason and severity. A file that opens with losses is a document of reduced fidelity, and this is where that is said.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string | yes | The CAD file to read. |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `cadmpeg_convert` — Write the file out in another format

Reads a CAD file and writes the same document to `out` as `step` (ISO 10303-21) or `cadir` (cadmpeg's own JSON). Answers the export report: the entities written, and what the target could not carry. Writes the file you name and nothing else.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `format` | string | yes | An output format this build carries, e.g. `step`. |
| `out` | string | yes | Where to write it. |
| `path` | string | yes | The CAD file to read. |
| `target` | string | no | A dialect inside the format, e.g. `ap242` for STEP. Omit to keep the dialect the document was read in. |


**destructive.**


## quiddity

**quiddity** — the geometry: feature recognition (bosses, holes, risers, pockets, chamfers), the frames a sensor perceives, and the exact surface underneath a feature.

### `quiddity_part` — What a STEP part is

Opens a STEP file and says what it holds: bodies, faces, edges, the bounding box in millimetres, whether each solid is valid, and the file's digest. Ask this first — every other tool takes the same path.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string | yes | Path to a STEP file (.step, .stp, either gzipped). |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `quiddity_features` — The part's manufacturing features

Recognises the part's features from the B-rep alone: holes (through, blind, counterbored, countersunk), pockets, slots, steps, bosses, patterns, fillets, chamfers, grooves, channels, sheet-metal and turned features — each with its measured size, position and the faces it is made of, and whether the evidence was proved. Also says what every face is: part of a feature, part of the body, refused, or unexplained. Optional `family` narrows to one family.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string | yes | Path to a STEP file (.step, .stp, either gzipped). |
| `family` | string | no | Only this family, e.g. `holes` or `pockets`. |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `quiddity_face` — One face of the part

What one face is: its surface (plane, cylinder with a radius, cone, sphere, torus, freeform), area, centroid, outward normal, neighbours, and which feature owns it. Faces are numbered 0 to face count − 1.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `face` | integer | yes | A face index. |
| `path` | string | yes | Path to a STEP file (.step, .stp, either gzipped). |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `quiddity_probe` — What is at a point, or under a ray

With `direction`: where a ray from `point` meets the part, nearest first — each hit naming the face, the point, outward normal and distance in millimetres. Without it: the faces nearest the point, which is how a coordinate becomes a face and then a feature.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string | yes | Path to a STEP file (.step, .stp, either gzipped). |
| `point` | list of number | yes | A point in millimetres, in the file's own coordinates. |
| `direction` | list of number | no | A ray direction. Omit to ask which faces are nearest. |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `quiddity_sense` — What a sensor sees at a pose

Puts a 64 × 64 sensor `distance` mm off the part, looking along `normal` (by default the outward normal of the face nearest `point`), and renders the frame against the exact B-rep. Answers coverage, the depth range, how many pixels met the part, and how much of the view each feature family covers.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string | yes | Path to a STEP file (.step, .stp, either gzipped). |
| `point` | list of number | yes | A point in millimetres, in the file's own coordinates. |
| `distance` | number | no | How far off the surface to stand, in millimetres (default 5). |
| `normal` | list of number | no | The surface normal to look along. Defaults to the nearest face's. |
| `resolution` | integer | no | Pixels a side (default 64). |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `quiddity_export_mjcf` — The part as a MuJoCo scene

Meshes the part and writes an MJCF model of it, in metres, for a physics simulator. The part keeps the place the file gives it; a body, its sensors and its actuators stay the experiment's. Writes the file you name.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `out` | string | yes | Where to write the MJCF. |
| `path` | string | yes | Path to a STEP file (.step, .stp, either gzipped). |
| `deflection` | number | no | Mesh chord tolerance in millimetres (default 0.05). |




### `quiddity_correspond` — What changed between two revisions

Compares two revisions of a part — each a STEP file or a recognition JSON file — and says what happened to each feature: carried unchanged, adapted (with what changed), orphaned, ambiguous, or new. It works when the part was moved or re-modelled, because it matches revision-independent fingerprints.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `new` | string | yes | The later revision. |
| `old` | string | yes | The earlier revision. |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**


## monty_cad

**monty_cad** — the memory: a sensed frame as the framework's own percept, and the labelled graph library a run loads.

### `monty_cad_brief` — What is this part?

Opens a STEP part and answers what quiddity recognised in it: the feature families and how many of each, the faces no feature claims, and how many records it could not prove. This is the sentence to read before asking a part anything else.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string | yes | the part to open |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `monty_cad_features_near` — Which features are near this point?

Opens a STEP part, recognises its features, and answers which of them sit within a radius of a point, nearest first — a hole, a boss, a chamfer by name and by distance. The distance is to the anchor the recognition gives a feature (a boss's axis point, for instance), not to its surface, so it orders features rather than measuring gaps.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string | yes | the part to open |
| `point` | list of number | yes | the point to measure from, in the part's millimetres |
| `limit` | integer | no | the most features to answer with (default 10) |
| `radius` | number | no | how far to look, in millimetres (default 25) |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `monty_cad_next_feature` — What is ahead?

Opens a STEP part, recognises its features, and answers which of them lie ahead of a point along a direction — within a cone, nearest first, with the distance and the angle off the direction for each. This is the move a policy makes when it jumps from one feature to the next.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `direction` | list of number | yes | which way the move goes, as three numbers |
| `path` | string | yes | the part to open |
| `point` | list of number | yes | where the move starts, in the part's millimetres |
| `angle` | number | no | how wide a cone counts as ahead, in degrees (default 45) |
| `limit` | integer | no | the most features to answer with (default 10) |
| `radius` | number | no | how far to look, in millimetres (default 500) |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `monty_cad_on_face` — What am I on?

Opens a STEP part and answers which feature claims a face — the id, the family and the feature's own parameters — or says that no feature claims it, and whether that is the body, a refusal, or a face the recognition could not explain. This is the question a sensor standing on the surface asks.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `face` | integer | yes | the face's own number, from 0 |
| `path` | string | yes | the part to open |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `monty_cad_sense` — What would the sensor perceive here?

Stands a patch sensor on the part at a point and looks along a direction, and answers what the framework's own observation processor makes of that frame: the node features a graph memory stores, which is the percept a run would have made at the same place.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `normal` | list of number | yes | which way it looks, as three numbers |
| `path` | string | yes | the part to sense |
| `point` | list of number | yes | where the sensor stands, in the part's own millimetres |
| `distance` | number | no | how far it stands off the surface, in millimetres |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `monty_cad_library` — Write the graph memory a run loads

Samples the part's surface, takes the percept at every visit, and writes the labelled library a run loads: gzipped JSON lines, one record per node, in the shape a graph learning module reads. The labels are the recognition's own, so they are facts rather than guesses.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `object` | string | yes | what the memory is called — the name a recognition would answer |
| `out` | string | yes | where to write the library |
| `path` | string | yes | the part to sample |
| `limit` | integer | no | the most visits to make |
| `spacing` | number | no | millimetres between visits |


**not idempotent: calling it twice is two effects.**

### `monty_cad_libraries` — What has this server already learned?

Answers the memories this server has written, newest first: the object each is labelled as, the part it was made from, how many nodes it holds, and where the file is. This is the question to ask before sampling a part again.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `limit` | integer | no | the most memories to answer with (default 20) |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**


## cluster

**cluster** — the plugins other nodes offer: experiments, learning modules and motor policies, whether this node answers the call or that one.

### `cad_plugin_list` — What does the cluster offer?

Lists the plugins registered across the cluster — experiments, learning modules and motor policies — with the node that offers each one. Optionally narrowed to one kind.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `kind` | string | no | only this kind |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**

### `cad_plugin_describe` — What is this plugin?

Asks one registered plugin what it says about itself: its version, whether it can be called from another node, and which engines it needs. A policy that reads a part must run where the part was opened, and this is where it says so.

| argument | type | required | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `kind` | string | yes | the kind it is registered as |
| `name` | string | yes | the plugin's name |
| `node` | string | no | ask on this node — an `:owner_only` plugin can only be called where its state is, and this is how a caller checks that the node holding its part offers it |


**read-only: it changes nothing.**


## What the server says about itself

Every `initialize` answer carries this text, before a model has asked anything:

> This server answers questions about a CAD part, and turns one into a graph memory that the Elixir Monty Studio can match against. A FILE: cadmpeg_formats says which formats this build reads and writes, and cadmpeg_inspect opens a path and answers the decode report — what was transferred and every loss with its reason. "It opened" and "it opened faithfully" are different answers. WHAT IS IN IT: monty_cad_brief opens the part and answers what quiddity recognised — the feature families and how many of each, and the faces no feature claims — which is the sentence a model needs before asking anything else. WHERE THE SENSOR WOULD STAND: monty_cad_sense takes a point and a direction and answers what the framework's own sensor module would perceive there: the node features a graph memory stores. WHICH FEATURE IS WHICH: monty_cad_on_face says what a face belongs to, monty_cad_features_near says what is around a point, and monty_cad_next_feature says what is ahead of one along a direction. Those three are the questions a policy asks before it chooses where to sense next. A MEMORY: monty_cad_library samples the part's surface, takes that percept at every visit, and writes the library a run loads — an object id, a node count, and how many nodes each feature family contributed. monty_cad_libraries says what has already been written, so a part is not sampled twice for nothing. THE GEOMETRY UNDERNEATH: the quiddity tools answer a face, a ray, a frame, a mesh and the surface samples directly, for a model that wants the numbers rather than a summary. WHAT A RUN IS MADE OF: cad_plugin_list says which experiments, learning modules and motor policies the cluster offers, and cad_plugin_describe asks one of them about itself — including whether it can be called from another node, which a policy that reads a part cannot. Paths are the interface. A native format that keeps parts of itself in files beside it is read against its own directory, which is why a file is named rather than bytes.
